summary.text: 走 is interpreted in early forms as a running person, and a clear verbal use meaning “run” is reported in Western Zhou bronze writing. In modern Chinese it commonly means “walk” or “go on foot.”

formation.text: The oldest proposed construction is pictographic: an early graph is interpreted as a person running with swinging arms. Some later bronze forms are analyzed as adding 止 to emphasize the feet. The received Shuowen account instead reads the seal-script form as 夭 plus 止, explaining 夭 as bending; this records a Han-era analysis and differs from the account of the earliest graph.

history.text: The graph is recorded in oracle-bone, bronze, Warring States, seal, clerical, and regular-script forms, with later forms increasingly altered. A modern digital rendering of the Shuowen seal-script tradition illustrates the received 夭-and-止 analysis; it does not establish the earliest structure.

In the standardized graph, the upper shape is 土 and the lower shape is 龰. These visible parts do not show that 土 was an original semantic component; the early upper figure is interpreted as a running person, later read as 夭 in the Shuowen tradition.

uncertainties.text: Analyses differ over whether the earliest graph depicts a running person and whether later bronze forms added 止. The Shuowen decomposition belongs to a separate historical analysis.

Oracle-bone examples are reported in place-name and personal-name contexts and do not establish an earlier verbal use. A clear verb meaning “run” is reported in a Western Zhou bronze inscription, but the evidence does not supply a securely dated first occurrence.
The documented senses of fleeing, going toward, and walking do not establish a complete chronology or a certain path of semantic development.

senses.text: A clear verbal use is reported in the bronze-inscription phrase 夙夜奔走. The cited oracle-bone examples are reported as names or place names, not secure verbal attestations.
Classical citations use 走 for fleeing or escaping. Their witnesses are not securely dated here, and they do not show when this sense developed in relation to “run.”
A historical sense “go or tend toward” is recorded, but the cited material does not establish its chronology relative to “run” or “flee.”
In modern use, 走 commonly means walking or going on foot. The evidence does not establish when this broader sense became current or how it developed from the older “run” sense.

limitations.text: The evidence supports a Western Zhou bronze use meaning “run,” but not a securely dated first use. The cited oracle-bone examples are not independently established as verbs.
The sources document fleeing, going toward, and walking, but do not establish their chronology or semantic connections.

overview.text: Early forms are interpreted as a person running with swinging arms. The character later appears with the meaning “run”; in modern Chinese it commonly means “walk” or “go on foot.”
